catalog_quote: Kanauji is a quantity sensitive language, and therefore stress assignment directly depends on the syllable weight. As in the Western Hindi, Kanauji of Kanpur exhibits three grades of syllable weight: light, heavy and super heavy. A syllable with one mora is considered to be light, while those with two and three morae are considered to be heavy and super heavy respectively. A short vowel contributes one mora and long vowel two to syllable weight. In a syllable, only coda consonants account for mora, and they each contribute one mora to its weight. Assuming that stress assignment takes place from right to left in Kanauji of Kanpur, a word receives stress according to following rules: • Maximally heavy syllable receives the stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes to the heaviest syllable of the word (light = 1 mora, heavy = 2, superheavy = 3; short V = 1 mora, long V/diphthong = 2, each coda C = 1). If two syllables tie for heaviest, the rightmost non-final of them wins; if all syllables are light, the rightmost non-final (penult) is stressed. Examples: [əʈərɪ'ja] 'roof' (final CVV heaviest), [ən'wad̪] 'quarrel' (final superheavy), [ə'ɡəʊɽa] tree name (two heavy syllables, rightmost non-final wins).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The authors say no dedicated study of Kanauji stress exists and that the rule is 'assumed' to apply right-to-left, modelled on Kelkar's (1968) Western Hindi rule; the final-syllable examples show that a final syllable can carry stress when it is uniquely heaviest.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms from the elicited wordlist, syllabified by the maximum onset principle); nothing on phrase-level stress. Describes Kanauji of Kanpur district.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes 'Kanauji of Kanpur' (Kanauji as spoken in Kanpur district, which the authors say is influenced by Bundeli, Awadhi, Braj and Bagheli); Glottolog treats Kanauji as the single language kana1281 (ISO bjj), so no separate glottocode applies. The authors flag that the rule is modelled on Kelkar's (1968) Western Hindi rule and 'assumed' to operate right-to-left, and that no dedicated study of Kanauji stress exists. Ahbab Khan's 2020 AMU thesis concerns 'Kannauji Urdu', a distinct variety, and was not read.

sources.note: Sec. 8 'Stress' (pp. 199-200): no dedicated study exists; Kanauji is quantity-sensitive with light/heavy/superheavy syllables; the maximally heavy syllable is stressed, ties go to the rightmost non-final, all-light words stress the rightmost non-final (Kelkar 1968-style Hindi rule, assumed right-to-left); three worked examples. Full text read via the Internet Archive copy of the academia.edu record (live academia/ResearchGate could not be reached by automated download).
